I'll really dumb it down and tell me if I went too far. I'd give the linked answer a read after you've been primed by my introduction.

One way of looking at mathematics is in terms of computation on a theoretical computer (Turing machine: a state machine that performs operations). Beyond obviously discovered stuff like the value of the finite calculation I showed above, there's a problem called the halting problem. Basically it asks if a program run on such a computer (infinite memory) would run in finite time. While it sounds odd, this is a very meaningful question and you can Google halting problem if you want to learn more. But many complicated problems are halting problems and this class is also almost universally believed to be discovered (i.e., the program either halts or not in reality and math). Intuitionists stop before this and only believe the finite stuff is discovered. They'd argue a halting problem could be unprovable and because if the lack of infinite time to test, couldn't be determined to halt or not. This position is hard to argue, but most are comfortable going further.

Going one step further, we have the arithmetic hierarchy. Basically these are problems that can't be stated in terms of a halting program. In fact, they each require you to solve an infinite number of halting problems. Consider this a halting problem for a computer that has access to the solution to the halting problem already. It's one step higher that way (like area vs. length). Most believe this still perfectly corresponds to reality and is thus discovered.

The hyperarithmetic hierarchy. The hyperarithmetic hierarchy is to the arithmetic hierarchy as the arithmetic hierarchy is to the halting problem. It's another step up where you have to solve an infinite number of the simpler class and that turns into a higher level halting problem too. This one is also believed to be discovered by most.

The author puts their limit at the Church Kleene ordinal which is the limit of countable computable ordinals. Beyond this problems aren't just ever more layers of halting problem. Anything beyond this he'd say is invented.

A very similar position is to exclude all uncountable sets as inventions (i.e., not real in nature ). The smallest such would be the union of all countable ordinals. So all uncountable sets, like the set of real numbers would be inventions. Not everyone agrees though. This position was popular before the discovery/invention of the Church Kleene ordinal.

The next stop is continuum and here most mathematicians are cautious. Things like the set of all functions on the Real line or Complex plane are too big for human intuition and there are problems on the continuum that can't be decided by very persuasive methods. This indicates this system may not be absolutely true or axiomatic. It's hard for anyone to say if this is discovered or invented if they didn't stop above at computable.

Beyond this we get very deep in to set theory and I can't summarize his answer accurately. Even the most die hard Platonists and logicians start dropping off rapidly and agree it's invented.

The limit would be set of all sets and ordinal of all ordinals. These concepts were proven inconsistent so while they may be useful inventions for some applications, they're not a discovered truth about our universe/logic.
